## The two delta symbols

Equation 6 weights each event contribution by the number of usable gaps for the subject who generated that event. The notation can be confusing because the equation uses both an uppercase and a lowercase delta:

- \(\Delta_{ij}\) is the event indicator. It is the quantity divided by \(m_i^*\).
- \(\delta_i\) is the group indicator. It stays unchanged.

Thus, the substitution is \(\Delta_{ij} \mapsto \Delta_{ij}/m_i^*\), not \(\delta_i \mapsto \delta_i/m_i^*\). Equation 6 uses \(m_i^*\), the paper's adjusted count of usable gaps, rather than the unadjusted \(m_i\).

## Applying the substitution to the second term

Write the event-level part of the second term in Equation 5 as

\[
q_{i'j'} = \Delta_{i'j'} L(\tilde t_{i'j'})
\left\{
  \delta_{i'} -
  \frac{Y_1(\tilde t_{i'j'})}{Y(\tilde t_{i'j'})}
\right\}.
\]

The second term is then

\[
\sum_{i'=1}^{n}\sum_{j'=1}^{m_{i'}}
q_{i'j'}\,
\frac{Y_{g_i i}(\tilde t_{i'j'})}{Y(\tilde t_{i'j'})}.
\]

In Equation 6, the event-level quantity is replaced by its Wang--Chang weighted version and divided by the gap count of its source subject:

\[
\sum_{i'=1}^{n}\sum_{j'=1}^{m_{i'}}
\frac{q^*_{i'j'}}{m_{i'}^*}\,
\frac{Y^*_{g_i i}(\tilde t_{i'j'})}{Y^*(\tilde t_{i'j'})},
\]

where

\[
q^*_{i'j'} = \Delta_{i'j'} L^*(\tilde t_{i'j'})
\left\{
  \delta_{i'} -
  \frac{Y_1^*(\tilde t_{i'j'})}{Y^*(\tilde t_{i'j'})}
\right\}.
\]

\newpage

For any fixed subject \(i'\), the value \(m_{i'}^*\) is constant over that subject's event index \(j'\). So that subject's contribution can be written as

\[
\frac{1}{m_{i'}^*}
\sum_{j'=1}^{m_{i'}}
q^*_{i'j'}\,
\frac{Y^*_{g_i i}(\tilde t_{i'j'})}{Y^*(\tilde t_{i'j'})}.
\]

This is the key step: \(1/m_{i'}^*\) is a denominator for each source subject's inner sum. Since different subjects can have different values of \(m_{i'}^*\), there is no single denominator to pull in front of the full double sum.

## Why the first term looks different

The first term is indexed over events from one focal subject \(i\). Its factor \(1/m_i^*\) is therefore common to that entire sum over \(j\):

\[
\frac{1}{m_i^*}\sum_{j=1}^{m_i}(\text{weighted event contribution for subject }i).
\]

In the second term, the outer sum runs over many source subjects \(i'\), each with its own denominator \(m_{i'}^*\). You can factor the denominator outside each subject's inner sum, but not outside the sum over subjects.

The package represents these subject-specific weights inside the weighted risk and event increments, so the factor \(1/m_i^*\) may not appear as a separate denominator in every later expression.
